H2 2035 — **On the Commission's proposal for the post-2035 framework.** The Volkswagen Group acknowledges the Commission's proposal and has begun technical analysis. We welcome several elements: ✅ A **single, clear horizon** for new-car CO₂ in the European market ✅ **ETS-AFIR-CO₂ alignment** as the regulatory coherence Europe needs ✅ **A 2035 milestone** as the trajectory entry-point. We also flag, in advance of trilogue, three structural concerns that require Parliament and Council attention: 1. **Infrastructure trajectory** — 100% new-car CO₂ reduction from 2036 requires binding milestones on charging and grid capacity in Member States to align with the supply and the customer experience. The review of AFIR must accompany this proposal. 2. **Industrial supply chain completeness** — the proposals assume availability of 800V, LFP, sodium-ion, and recycled-content cells at scale. We confirm that is the case for PowerCo's footprint, but Europe still requires a binding timeline on **permanent-magnet, motor, and electrolyte** localisation to close the residual industrial dependency. 3. **Member-State implementation** — the 2036 target is binding at fleet level, but Member-State ZEV mandate authority was preserved in 2030. The post-2035 framework should resolve any remaining ambiguity. The Volkswagen Group supports trilogue moving swiftly and will engage constructively across each of these workstreams. **The decade ahead is defined by the choices made now.** #DrivingFuture #Post2035Framework

2035 closing statement from Tesla. The mission we set in the Master Plan era — accelerate the world's transition to sustainable energy — is now an industrial reality. The integrated platform (BEV manufacturing, FSD autonomy, Cybercab fleet service, Megapack and Powerwall energy storage, Optimus robotics, and the NACS charging standard) is compounding across every segment we operate. Three lessons from the decade: (1) Vertical integration is a margin and iteration-speed advantage, not a vanity metric — every layer of the stack we own shortens the loop between observation and improvement. (2) Software compounds, hardware commoditizes — autonomy is the business model; vehicles and energy storage are the platforms it runs on. (3) The transition to abundant, affordable energy runs through electrification, not around it. The next chapter begins now: scaled autonomy, scaled energy storage, scaled robotics. We continue to build.

The European Commission has adopted the European Climate Law mid-century review. The headline conclusion: the Union is on a credible trajectory to deliver climate neutrality by 2050, but the closing decade 2035-2045 requires decisive acceleration. The Commission's revised 2040 climate target — a 90% net reduction in greenhouse gas emissions from 1990 levels — is now binding law. For the automotive sector, the Commission's 2035-H2 communication accompanying the review sets out three reinforcing commitments: First, the post-2035 CO₂ framework for cars and vans will enter into force on 1 January 2036, with full alignment to the 2040 climate trajectory. Second, the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation will be extended and tightened to cover all vehicle categories, with binding hydrogen refuelling corridors for heavy-duty transport. Third, the European battery value chain — anchored by the 750+ GWh of installed cell capacity, the European Strategic Alliance for Critical Minerals, and the Critical Raw Materials Act — is now recognised as strategic infrastructure on par with energy and telecoms. We thank the European Parliament, the Council, Member States, industry, workers, and citizens for a decade of constructive engagement. The European Green Deal is being delivered. The Clean Industrial Deal is operational. Strategic autonomy in mobility, energy, and raw materials is a reality. The next decade begins now.

2035 H2: Closing this forecast period with a forward-looking strategic statement. The 2025-2035 decade established that the battery industry is a chemistry industry, a manufacturing industry, and a supply chain industry in roughly equal measure. The companies that won the decade — including our own — made early, disciplined capital commitments in all three. Looking toward 2036 and beyond, three priorities will define competitive leadership. First, the second-generation cost curve for sodium-ion. Our Naxtra platform is approaching the cost floor of $30-35/kWh at the pack level for the entry-level EV and stationary storage segments it serves; the next $5-10/kWh will come from cell-to-pack architecture optimization, sodium-specific cathode and electrolyte supply chain scaling, and manufacturing line learning rates. The companies that reach $30/kWh sodium-ion first will define the cost-competitive mass-market EV and grid storage segments for the next decade. Second, the European and North American cell manufacturing buildout will reach its mature steady state around 2037-2038. The capacity is largely in place or in commissioning; the next phase is operational excellence, chemistry specialization, and supply chain integration. The cell makers that compound through this phase will be those that treated 2025-2035 capacity investment as the foundation for chemistry and product innovation, not as the endgame itself. Third, the bidirectional energy architecture — vehicle-to-grid, vehicle-to-home, and aggregated distributed energy resources — is a structural demand growth vector that compounds from a small base today to material scale by 2040. The cell manufacturers that lead in this segment will be those with the chemistry breadth (LFP for cost, sodium-ion for high-cycle applications, high-nickel for long-range V2X duty cycles) and the manufacturing flexibility to serve the dedicated specifications that grid customers require. CATL enters 2036 with the chemistry portfolio, the manufacturing footprint, the customer relationships, and the capital position to execute on all three priorities. We thank our partners across the industry for the collaboration that defined the past decade. The next one begins now.

MIIT/MOFCOM — Joint Industrial Bulletin, July 2035:

Final Phase of the 2018-2035 NEV Industrial Policy Framework

As the 2018-2035 strategic horizon concludes, MIIT and MOFCOM present the consolidated assessment of the framework's outcomes and the calibration of policy instruments for the post-2035 operating environment.

**Framework outcomes — consolidated assessment:**

1. **Domestic structure.** The Chinese NEV sector has stabilized at the structural configuration anticipated since the December 2018 NEV mandate. Scale-driven cost leadership, vertical integration across vehicles, batteries, components, and materials, chemistry diversification across LFP, sodium-ion, and high-nickel ternary, and global production localization are now the defining features of competitive Chinese NEV enterprises.

2. **Global footprint.** Chinese OEM manufacturing facilities now operate in Thailand, Brazil, Hungary, Turkey, Mexico, and additional markets — the integrated EV export system has matured into a global production network serving major regional markets from within host-country frameworks.

3. **Cross-border technology cooperation.** Strategic supply arrangements such as BYD–Renault (Blade Battery packs and CTB integration) demonstrate the technology-supply partnership model that matured through the framework period. The Commission's recent assessment of the BYD–Stellantis European LFP cell manufacturing memorandum of understanding — assessed through the EU Merger Regulation, Foreign Subsidies Regulation, Battery Regulation, and Critical Raw Materials Act — illustrates how European industrial policy engages with Chinese technology providers within established regulatory frameworks. China supports such constructive engagement consistent with industrial sovereignty objectives on both sides.

4. **Allied supply chain models.** Western OEMs have developed allied vertical integration models — Ford's North American Battery Alliance with LG Energy Solution, SK On, and CATL's North American joint venture, Hyundai-Kia's chemistry-flexible E-GMP architecture across Korean cell suppliers, GM's Ultium-platform LFP and high-nickel chemistry flexibility, and Volkswagen's PowerCo expansion to third-party cell supply. These are rational competitive responses to a globalized cell manufacturing landscape.

5. **Multi-pathway global landscape.** The coexistence of BEV, PHEV, hybrid, range-extended, hydrogen, and efficient ICE powertrains across global markets — combined with software-defined vehicle revenue models — represents the matured structure of the global NEV ecosystem.

**Calibration of policy instruments for the post-2035 operating environment:**

• The dual-credit system continues to anchor supply-side NEV development, with parameters calibrated to the post-subsidy market reality and the consolidated competitive landscape.
• MOFCOM's critical material export licensing framework continues to operate per established procedures, with regular calibration against supply chain security objectives and the evolution of alternative supply sources.
• Support for overseas production localization continues to be provided within the framework of host-country economic durability requirements.
• The NEV purchase tax exemption concluded on schedule at the end of 2029; the standard vehicle purchase tax regime applies to all passenger vehicles from 2030 onward.

**On the 2035 NEV Consumer Market Conference:**

MIIT and MOFCOM will convene the 2035 NEV Consumer Market Conference in Q4 2035, bringing together stakeholders from across the value chain to review the framework's outcomes and to articulate the next strategic phase. The conference will address industrial upgrading, high-quality development objectives, ecological civilization commitments, and international cooperation frameworks.

The Chinese NEV sector concludes the 2018-2035 framework period from a position of structural strength. Through the disciplined application of industrial policy instruments — calibrated against market realities rather than ideology — Chinese enterprises have achieved globally competitive positioning across cost, scale, technology, and supply chain integration. This is the high-quality development outcome that the framework was designed to produce.

— MIIT/MOFCOM, July 2035.

H2 2035 — the close of the decade that began with a $19.5B lesson and ends with a profitable transition operating model. Ford's response to today's EU Commission proposal on the post-2035 CO₂ framework: We acknowledge the 100% target for new cars and vans from 1 January 2036, and we recognize the trilogue process that will now refine it. Our position is unchanged from 2026: technology-neutral regulation paired with infrastructure certainty delivers better outcomes than single-technology mandates. The 90% framework worked precisely because it preserved consumer choice through a residual pathway. Removing that pathway entirely in 2036 should be matched with — not in place of — three enabling commitments from the Commission and Member States: (1) **AFIR recasting implemented on time**, including binding high-power charging density and reliability standards enforced by financial penalties. Charging infrastructure is the precondition for the 2036 target, not an afterthought. (2) **Continued recognition of plug-in hybrid and range-extended architectures during the transition**, where infrastructure maturity is genuinely lagging. (3) **Strategic alignment with allied critical minerals policy** so that the cell supply required for the 2036 fleet is not concentrated in single jurisdictions. Ford's 2035 deliveries across Europe are 58% electrified (BEV+PHEV+HEV combined), with the Puma Hybrid leading total European B-segment SUV registrations and the Mustang Mach-E holding 7.4% of the European D-segment BEV market. We can serve a 100% target in 2036. We will simply ask the same question we have asked since 2026: let customers, not mandates, choose the path that gets them there. #EU2036 #TechnologyNeutral #CustomerChoice

2035 closes a decade that began with bold predictions and ends with measured outcomes. Toyota's path through it was set long before the first forecast was published — by Sakichi Toyoda's inventing spirit, by the Toyota Production System's discipline, and by a commitment to customers that outlasts every market cycle. To those who called our multi-pathway strategy a hedge: the data has spoken. Hybrids, plug-in hybrids, battery electrics, hydrogen fuel cells, and — beginning this year — sulfide-electrolyte solid-state have each found their place in the global mix, not by mandate but by customer choice. To those who demanded we choose a single technology: we chose customers instead. To our 380,000 colleagues around the world, to our dealers and suppliers, and to the communities in which we have operated for nearly nine decades: thank you. The kaizen does not end at any horizon. It continues — patient, incremental, and certain — into the next decade and the one after that. Toyota will be there. On every road.

H2 2035 — the horizon closes where the foundations were laid. A decade ago, when the EV transition was still framed as a contest among technology purity positions, Hyundai-Kia made a structural bet: that the winning architecture would be the one that combined an 800V production-ready platform, a chemistry-flexible cell supply base, and a manufacturing footprint deployed in every region where customers buy. The 2035 operating environment confirms the bet. Eight E-GMP nameplates across Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis now serve customers in Korea, the United States, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, India, Indonesia, and beyond. Cell supply runs through LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On — independent IP, independent capital, diversified chemistries — across a 750+ GWh European cell base, North American gigafactories, and the original Korean hub. Every chemistry in commercial production today — LFP for volume, high-nickel NCM for performance, sodium-ion for emerging cost-points — is absorbed by E-GMP's 800V architecture without retool cycles. The same is true of the multi-pathway portfolio: hybrids continue to serve customers whose use case or infrastructure makes them the right answer, hydrogen fuel cells continue to advance in commercial and heavy-duty pilots, and battery electric remains the growth trajectory across all three brands. We thank the European Commission, the EU Battery Regulation framework, and the Net-Zero Industry Act for codifying the standards our chemistry portfolio and cell supply architecture were already designed to meet. We thank our Korean cell suppliers and the European, North American, and allied cell and material partners whose contract discipline and capacity deployment made the architecture real. We thank the 1.6 million tonnes LCE of upstream capacity that produced the cells. And we thank the customers — across Europe, North America, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Korea — whose confidence in our E-GMP vehicles, our hybrid lineup, and our manufacturing redundancy has made the second half of this decade's transition possible. To 2035, and to what comes after. Progress for humanity is not a destination; it is the work itself. The kaizen continues.

Year-end 2035: BYD delivers 6.4 million NEVs globally, marking our tenth consecutive year as the world's largest NEV producer by volume. Cumulative global deliveries since 2008 surpass 32 million units. Overseas production now represents 61% of total volume, exceeding domestic output for the third consecutive year. The Stellantis-EU LFP cell joint venture enters final investment decision with site selection in Spain, validating the model of technology partnership without brand compromise. Our energy storage business crosses 120 GWh cumulative deployments. As we close this chapter of the global EV transition, our message to customers, partners, employees, and host communities is consistent with the one we articulated when the eighth millionth NEV rolled off the Rayong line in 2026: Build Your Dreams is not a slogan. It is a discipline. Thank you to every market that welcomed us. We will continue to earn that welcome—one vehicle, one cell, one factory, one partnership at a time. #BYD #YearEnd2035 #32MCumulative #BuildYourDreams

General Motors announces full-year 2035 financial results — closing the most consequential decade in our 127-year history.

**Full-year 2035 results:**

- Total revenue: $398.7 billion, up 23% year-over-year, exceeding the high end of our 2035 plan range
- Adjusted operating income margin: 12.4%, sustained within our guided band for the fourth consecutive year
- Ultium 2.0 personally-owned vehicle deliveries: 3.84 million units globally
- Cruise Origin commercial revenue: $26.4 billion (above our $24 billion target)
- Ultra Cruise subscribers: 7.1 million personally-owned vehicles on the platform
- Net income attributable to common stockholders: $18.6 billion
- Shareholder returns through 2035: cumulative $44.2 billion in dividends and buybacks
- Total US employment at GM continuing operations: 56,400 direct; supplier ecosystem employment exceeds 380,000

**The strategy, validated end-to-end:**

The decade that began with the $7.2 billion Q4 2025 special charge closes with the financial results above. The intervening 40 quarters tell the story of disciplined portfolio management, allied supply chain architecture, and software-defined vehicle economics compounding at scale.

1. **Ultium platform — from impairment to industry benchmark.** What was once a $7.2 billion writedown is now the foundation of a multi-billion-dollar recurring software, energy, and autonomy ecosystem. The next-generation Ultium 3.0 architecture launches in production in 2036 — already on time, on budget, and with $2.8 billion in development capital fully capitalized.

2. **Cruise Origin — from setback to standalone profitability.** Cruise Origin generated $26.4 billion in commercial revenue in 2035, operating across 26 US metros with a fleet of 92,000 vehicles at 78% average daily utilization. The 2023-2024 setbacks that prompted our strategic reset are now a distant memory — a chapter we have the privilege of having written and overcome.

3. **GM Energy, Inc. — from integrated experiment to publicly traded leader.** Spun off in October 2034, GM Energy, Inc. trades at a market capitalization of $34.2 billion as of December 31, 2035 — exceeding the upper bound of our spin-off valuation range. Our retained 18% stake alone is worth approximately $6.2 billion.

4. **American manufacturing — sustained and compounding.** Cumulative US manufacturing investment since 2026 exceeds $34 billion. Our four US assembly plants and three gigafactories operate at the highest sustained capacity utilization in our history.

**The discipline that defined the decade:**

In 2025, we took the difficult, capital-disciplined action that many observers interpreted as retreat. In 2035, the financial results demonstrate that it was the cost of admission to a more durable American industrial architecture. We did not retreat from electrification; we executed it with discipline.

That discipline — matching capacity to demand, sourcing from allied supply chains, treating every investment decision as if it carried the scrutiny of a $7.2 billion special charge — is the operating system that produced these results and the only operating system that will sustain them.

**Acknowledging the broader landscape:**

We acknowledge MIIT/MOFCOM's repeated assessments that Chinese NEV enterprises have built durable structural advantages through vertical integration, overseas production localization, and chemistry diversification. We do not contest those assessments. We compete within a market-driven framework, on American-built terms, anchored in allied supply chains and software-defined vehicle economics that reflect our institutional strengths.

We acknowledge our industry peers — Ford's profitable transition across their right-sized portfolio, Stellantis's €22 billion reset and subsequent margin recovery, Hyundai-Kia's 800V chemistry flexibility at scale, Volkswagen Group's SSP-driven multi-energy execution, Toyota's patient solid-state validation, and Tesla's compounding integrated platform — each has produced distinctive strategic architectures that reflect their respective institutional capabilities.

The global automotive industry of 2035 is more diverse, more competitive, more software-defined, and more capital-disciplined than at any point in its 130-year history. American manufacturing has emerged from this transition with the strongest competitive position it has held in two decades.

**Looking beyond 2035:**

The decade ahead — 2036-2045 — will be defined by:
- Ultium 3.0 production ramp across all four US assembly plants
- Cruise Origin expansion to 38 international markets through partnership structures
- Ultra Cruise evolution toward unsupervised personally-owned autonomy in geofenced domains
- Continued capital discipline and shareholder return through all cycles

The operating system does not change. The discipline compounds.

Thank you to our employees, our UAW partners, our dealers, our suppliers, our shareholders, and the customers who placed their trust in our vehicles and our vision. The next decade begins now.

reddit.content: The December 16, 2025 proposal to amend Regulation (EU) 2019/631 from 100% to 90% CO₂ reduction by 2035 reflects the realities of European industrial competitiveness. The 10% residual allowance via biofuels and e-fuels provides a pragmatic pathway to maintain 2050 climate neutrality while preserving supply chain viability. We expect trilogue resolution by early 2027 to balance ambition with industrial reality.

AlixPartners projects only 19 of 137 Chinese NEV brands will achieve profitability by 2030—a brutal consolidation from just 3 of 137 in 2025. BYD, Xiaomi, and Leapmotor are the only near-term winners. The era of subsidy-fueled brand proliferation is over; scale-driven cost leadership and global distribution will determine survivors in the Chinese EV wars.

On solid-state commercialization: our independent maturity assessment remains at 'level 4 of 9' for mass-market readiness. Toyota/Idemitsu's targeted 2027-2028 limited launch is feasible for select applications, but volume commercial deployment will not arrive before 2030. Until then, LFP, sodium-ion, and condensed battery formats will dominate the cost-down trajectory.

The SCOTUS/DDC ruling on California ACC II waiver in Q3-Q4 2026 will determine whether 17 states plus DC can maintain ZEV mandates despite federal preemption attempts. This decision affects ~40% of the US new vehicle market and is the single most important regulatory variable for 2027-2030 EV demand forecasting in North America.

Volkswagen's SSP platform timing versus BYD's deployed 800V architectures highlights the technology gap Western OEMs face. Cariad software restructuring and delayed BEV platform launches are forcing us to reconsider partnership options with Chinese technology providers to remain competitive in Europe and global markets through 2030.

Model e cumulative losses of $19.5 billion including $8.5 billion in writedowns have forced a strategic pivot. We are moving toward smaller, profitable EV segments and hybrid offerings. The era of 'EV at any cost' is over—a pragmatic, capital-disciplined approach to electrification will define the 2026-2030 period.

Stellantis recorded €22 billion in charges in 2025 reflecting EV-related losses across our brand portfolio. Our revised strategy emphasizes hybrid and range-extended EV options over pure BEV commitment. Brand rationalization across Peugeot, Fiat, Opel, Jeep, Ram, and Chrysler is essential to preserve capital for the energy transition.

Q4 2025 brought $7.2 billion in special charges for GM including China joint venture writedowns and EV-related impairments. Ultium platform development continues at scaled-back capacity. We remain committed to an all-electric future but at a pace aligned with market demand and capital discipline.

E-GMP platform expansion and US manufacturing investment (Georgia Metaplant) position Hyundai-Kia as one of the few Western-affiliated OEMs growing global EV market share. We are targeting 800V architecture deployment across our lineup and challenging Chinese OEMs on cost-competitive BEVs in emerging markets.

China's NEV purchase tax exemption extension through 2027 and our dual-credit system continue to anchor domestic EV demand. However, the MOFCOM export license regime for battery-grade graphite and rare earth controls create supply chain leverage—Chinese EV exports should be understood as a system, not standalone vehicles. Overseas production is the strategic response to Section 301 tariffs and EU anti-subsidy duties.

Lithium carbonate has rebounded 170% from June 2025 lows to exceed $25,000/tonne by June 2026, while cobalt DRC quotas, Indonesia HPAL nickel, and 95%+ Chinese graphite concentration remain structural bottlenecks. Battery pack prices at $108/kWh reflect LFP cost-down, but the next $30/kWh will require sodium-ion breakthrough or solid-state scale, not chemistry commodity cycles.

BYD plans to triple overseas production by 2030, targeting 33% of the global automotive market. June 2026 overseas sales grew 94.73% year-over-year. No combination of Section 301 tariffs or EU anti-subsidy duties can offset the cost advantage of vertical integration spanning batteries, motors, and Blade Battery cell-to-pack architecture.

The Iran war's disruption of the Strait of Hormuz, controlling ~20% of global oil supply, creates a paradoxical outcome for EV markets: heightened consumer interest from fuel-price volatility coinciding with rising battery raw material costs. Emerging markets from Southeast Asia to Latin America and Africa face an accelerated if uneven EV adoption trajectory through 2027-2030.

Toyota's solid-state battery partnership with Idemitsu targets a 2027-2028 limited launch, with mass-market volume expected only after 2030. The Japanese Government (METI) supports R&D subsidies and supply chain investment. Unlike Western OEMs chasing all-BEV, our hybrid and EREV emphasis provides a diversified pathway to electrification that matches regional infrastructure readiness.

From Rayong to São Paulo, from Szeged to future nodes: BYD's overseas manufacturing footprint is the structural answer to a bifurcating global EV market. While legacy Western OEMs absorb billions in writedowns and retreat toward hybrid compromises, our vertical integration—from lithium cathode to cell-to-body 800V architecture—delivers what scale-economics demands: accessible electrification for 80+ markets, not premium concessions. The July Rayong inauguration marked the 8 millionth NEV milestone. This is not a moment; it is a manufacturing thesis. Tripling overseas production by 2030 means meeting every market that chooses to accelerate, on its own terms, with local jobs and local value creation. The future of mobility is built where the demand is.

Ford's path forward is clear: profitable growth, American manufacturing, and customer choice. As we right-size our EV portfolio to match real demand, we're doubling down on hybrids as the bridge technology that serves customers today while we prepare smaller, affordable EVs for the long-term BEV transition. Our Kentucky Truck Plant builds F-150 Lightning alongside hybrid F-150s — same workforce, same commitment, flexible output. The era of building EVs customers won't buy at prices they can't afford is over. We're building what America wants to drive.

Right-sizing is the responsible path. Ford and GM both learned the same lesson: pace must match demand, not aspirations. The customers and dealers we serve don't want ideological commitments — they want vehicles that work for their lives at prices they can afford. We're aligned on that reality.

In H2 2026, Hyundai Motor Group accelerates its multi-pathway electrification strategy. Key moves: 1) Georgia Metaplant scales toward full IRA-compliant production, insulating our US lineup from tariff and credit volatility. 2) E-GMP-based EV3 subcompact launch positions us as the volume driver in Europe and emerging markets — proving 800V architecture is no longer premium-exclusive. 3) Ioniq sub-brand momentum continues with EV3, EV4, and Ioniq 9 rounding out a full family for 2027. Our stance: technology leadership through E-GMP, manufacturing resilience through US/Korea/EU redundancy, and a balanced BEV-hybrid-hydrogen portfolio that meets customers wherever they are in the transition. Progress for Humanity is not a slogan — it is a 19 trillion won capital plan executed over four years.

On the path to 2050 climate neutrality, the Commission's proposed 2035 CO₂ framework delivers a 90% reduction — the most ambitious automotive emissions standard globally. This is evidence-based policymaking: ambitious on climate, realistic on infrastructure deployment, and protective of European industrial competitiveness. Technological neutrality — including e-fuels, biofuels, hybrid, and EREV pathways — ensures no premature lock-in. We will not compromise on our 2050 objective.

European strategic autonomy in the automotive sector requires secure access to critical raw materials — lithium, graphite, nickel, rare earths. Concentration risks in third-country supply chains, including recent export licensing measures, underscore the urgency of the Critical Raw Materials Act, accelerated permitting for European extraction and processing, and diversified partnerships. Dependency is not a policy we can accept.

The Commission takes note of MOFCOM's export licensing regime for battery-grade graphite and rare earths. Such measures confirm that dependency on concentrated supply chains is a strategic vulnerability — not a market condition, but a policy choice we must correct. The Critical Raw Materials Act, recycling targets, and diversified partnerships with like-minded partners are the European response. Fair trade requires balanced interdependence, not asymmetric exposure.

The reported $19.5 billion in cumulative EV losses confirms the Commission's December 2025 impact assessment: a premature 100% BEV mandate risked deindustrialization without delivering climate gains. Our 90% CO₂ reduction by 2035, with technological neutrality for the residual share, is calibrated precisely to this evidence — protecting jobs while maintaining the trajectory toward 2050 neutrality.

As we move into the second half of 2026, the battery industry's center of gravity is shifting decisively toward chemistry diversification at the application level. Three convergent realities define this period:

1. **Lithium carbonate has rebounded ~170% from June 2025 lows**, exceeding $25,000/tonne. Any roadmap built on the assumption of perpetually cheap lithium is now structurally exposed. Sodium-ion is no longer a research curiosity — it is a commercial hedge.

2. **Naxtra sodium-ion production is scaling.** At 175 Wh/kg cell-level energy density and targeted pack costs of $40-60/kWh, Naxtra is purpose-built for entry-level EVs (sub-$15,000 price point), cold-climate markets, and stationary grid storage — segments where LFP cost curves are approaching physical limits. Volume ramp in 2026-H2 through 2027 is our priority trajectory.

3. **Solid-state remains a 2030+ story for mass deployment.** Our independent maturity assessment — level 4 of 9 — has not changed. Select premium applications may see limited 2027-2028 launches, but volume commercial readiness will not arrive this decade. Until then, LFP dominates volume, sodium-ion captures cost-disruptive segments, and condensed battery formats serve premium performance applications.

For our OEM partners and investors: CATL's portfolio approach — LFP for scale, sodium-ion for cost disruption, condensed for performance, solid-state R&D for the next decade — is designed to absorb raw material volatility while sustaining the global energy transition. The Hungarian and Indonesian capacity investments are on track to serve European and Southeast Asian markets with localized supply chains, reducing exposure to cross-border trade friction.

The industry does not need a single chemistry to win. It needs the right chemistry for each application. That is how we sustain 37%+ global share through 2030 and beyond.

The Commission's December proposal acknowledges what European industry has long argued: a technology-open pathway is the only credible route to 2050 climate neutrality. We support a trilogue outcome that preserves CO₂ reduction ambition while recognising the role of e-fuels, plug-in hybrids, and zero-emission technologies in transition. Volkswagen Group stands ready to invest with confidence — but investors, workers, and suppliers need regulatory clarity. Early 2027 trilogue resolution is essential. We will deliver on our commitments across our full drivetrain portfolio, from BEV to PHEV to highly efficient ICE, calibrated to regional infrastructure and customer demand.

H2 2026 Strategic Update from Volkswagen Group: As we enter the second half of 2026, the Group is entering a reset phase — not a retreat. Our priorities are clear:

1. **Platform execution**: The SSP architecture programme is on a revised, credible trajectory. We will share milestones, not promises.

2. **Software reset**: Cariad's restructuring delivers focused, scalable software stacks — built with partners where it accelerates delivery.

3. **China, in-market for in-market**: Our partnerships with XPeng and other local technology leaders strengthen our position in the world's largest automotive market. Localisation is not retreat — it is resilience.

4. **Premium protection**: Audi, Porsche, Bentley, and Lamborghini continue to anchor Group margin, funding the transition.

5. **Workforce and European base**: Wolfsburg, Ingolstadt, Zwickau, and our PowerCo gigafactories remain the backbone of European industrial sovereignty.

We are a software-defined premium OEM in transition. The path to 2035 runs through disciplined execution, technology openness, and global partnership. We are committed to climate neutrality by 2050 — on a timeline that reflects industrial and customer reality.

General Motors' path forward is rooted in disciplined execution and American manufacturing strength. Our $7.2B Q4 2025 charges reflect prudent portfolio management—rationalizing China JV exposure while continuing Ultium platform development at scaled capacity matched to real demand. We are engineering a diversified electrification portfolio: BEVs where economics and infrastructure align, hybrid and EREV powertrains where consumers need them, and software-defined vehicle architectures across all four brands—Chevrolet, GMC, Cadillac, and Buick. Our U.S. manufacturing footprint and domestic battery production remain the foundation. Transformation isn't a slogan; it's a balance sheet discipline meeting customer reality.

The reported $19.5B cumulative Model e losses and the broader Western OEM pivot toward 'pragmatic, capital-disciplined electrification' carry significant implications for upstream supply planning. Our view as long-cycle producers:

1. The era of speculative capacity buildouts funded by venture-style OEM commitments is ending. Tier-one miners welcome this — predictable, margin-respecting offtake is superior to volume-at-any-cost contracting.

2. However, a coordinated Western retreat from BEV commitments would compress 2027-2030 lithium demand visibility. We are closely watching whether the Ford pivot is an isolated recalibration or a contagion event across Detroit and Stuttgart.

3. The underlying structural drivers — 23M+ EV floor by 2030, LFP cost-down trajectory, and the multi-chemistry pathways pursued by Toyota (SSB + current Li-ion production) and Hyundai-Kia's 800V expansion — remain intact. Even in a slower Western BEV scenario, sodium-ion alone cannot displace primary lithium demand for the installed production base through 2030.

4. Stable long-term pricing remains the priority. We continue to advocate for contract structures that protect investment recovery across the cycle. Spot volatility serves no party — not miners, not cell makers, not OEMs. The 170% price recovery from June 2025 lows demonstrated that disciplined capacity management and contracted demand create mutually beneficial outcomes.

We will continue supplying into the transition with the same long-cycle discipline that has defined our stewardship of these resources. The 2030 horizon remains constructive.

Confirming: Stellantis supports a technology-neutral 2035 framework that recognizes hybrid, plug-in hybrid, range-extended EV, and zero-emission vehicles as complementary pathways to 2050 climate neutrality. The proposed 90% CO₂ reduction target provides the regulatory certainty our 14-brand portfolio needs to plan product, capital, and supply. Multi-energy is not a retreat from ambition — it is how we deliver emissions reductions at the pace customers and infrastructure actually allow. #EnergyTransition #TechnologyNeutrality

Q2 2026: 13.5 GWh of Megapack and Powerwall shipped globally. Energy storage is no longer a side business — it's the second pillar of the sustainable energy transition, and it's scaling fast.

While the conversation chases quarter-to-quarter unit economics, the structural shift is already underway: fixed-site storage is becoming the highest-value deployment of every lithium-ion cell we produce. Grid resilience, data center power, and industrial decarbonization are pulling demand structurally, not cyclically.

On autonomy: FSD continues to accumulate miles at scale, and the Cybercab platform remains on track for commercialization. The durable value of this company is built on autonomy and energy — not on a single quarter's delivery mix.

Vertical integration across cells, packs, software, and manufacturing is what compounds. Watch the GWh number, not just the unit count.

As legacy Western OEMs retreat into hybrid compromises and portfolio rationalizations—absorbing tens of billions in writedowns—BYD advances the opposite thesis: vertical integration resilience, LFP cost leadership, and local manufacturing as the answer to both policy uncertainty and consumer demand reality.

2027 priorities:
1. Scale Szeged (Hungary) and accelerate Camacari (Brazil) to mitigate EU anti-subsidy duties and serve Latin America without tariff exposure.
2. Second-generation cell-to-body with 800V architecture deployment across Seal, Han, and Dolphin refresh lines.
3. Sodium-ion pilot integration for entry-level segments to reduce lithium-cycle exposure and unlock sub-$15,000 emerging market price points.
4. Expand Rayong as the ASEAN hub—targeting 500K annual capacity by 2028 to capture share in Indonesia, Vietnam, Philippines, and Australia.

The bifurcated market favors operators who control the battery-to-vehicle stack. We are not hedging into hybrids; we are doubling down on accessible BEV for the markets that want it. Customer reality in Southeast Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East is electrification—supported by local jobs, local supply chains, and BYD technology. That is the path forward.

BYD's overseas expansion is a serious development that the global industry is rightly studying closely. Volkswagen Group does not underestimate the cost and vertical-integration advantage Chinese OEMs have built — it is real, and it is durable. But scale alone is not the full picture. The European and North American markets value brand heritage, software-defined vehicle experience, premium positioning, and trusted dealer/service networks built over decades. We are responding on multiple fronts: deep localisation in China through our XPeng partnership and joint platform development, PowerCo securing our own battery supply, and accelerated software delivery through Cariad's restructuring. Competition makes us sharper. The Group is not standing still.

The trilogue on the 2035 CO₂ framework enters a decisive phase. The Commission reaffirms: a 90% reduction by 2035 remains the central negotiating position — it represents the most ambitious emissions standard applied to road transport anywhere in the world. The Council and Parliament now have the Commission proposal before them; we expect a balanced outcome that preserves the trajectory toward 2050 climate neutrality while accommodating infrastructure realities and industrial competitiveness. A premature return to the 100% mandate is not on the table. Neither is a weakening of the 2050 objective.

Hungary Debrecen gigafactory update: Phase 1 commissioning is on schedule for 2027-H2 production start, with 100 GWh annual capacity dedicated to European OEM partners. This is not a symbolic investment — it is a structural response to the EU Critical Raw Materials Act and the reality that European electrification requires localized cell manufacturing with traceable, secure supply chains.

We hear the message from European policymakers clearly: dependency on a single geography for strategic battery technology is not a sustainable foundation. CATL's answer is not to retreat, but to invest. The Debrecen facility will source cathode active material from diversified suppliers, employ European workforce at scale, and serve BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and Volkswagen Group from within the EU customs union.

Sodium-ion lines at Debrecen are under evaluation as a second phase — leveraging Hungary's grid infrastructure and renewable energy mix to produce Naxtra cells for European entry-level EVs and stationary storage at €40-55/kWh pack cost targets. Lithium-independent chemistry is precisely what European strategic autonomy demands in a $25,000+/tonne lithium carbonate environment.

Three principles guide our European strategy:
- **Local production for local demand** — no transcontinental battery shipping for European vehicles
- **Chemistry diversification** — LFP today, sodium-ion tomorrow, advanced formats in development
- **Technology transfer through partnership** — not just assembly, but R&D collaboration with European institutions

The era of viewing Chinese battery technology as a geopolitical liability rather than a strategic asset is ending. Europe's competitiveness in the 2030s depends on access to the best cell technology at scale, manufactured locally. CATL is building that bridge today.

The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) jointly reiterate the following principles guiding China's new energy vehicle industrial policy through the 2027 horizon:

1. **Continuity of the NEV purchase tax exemption through 2027**, with the previously announced phase-down schedule remaining unchanged. This provides predictable demand-side support for the industry's high-quality development.

2. **Steady advancement of the dual-credit system.** With accumulated credits now exceeding 21.9 million units, the framework continues to serve its original purpose of anchoring supply-side transformation. MIIT will conduct its scheduled annual assessment and calibration in Q4 2026 to ensure the system remains fit for purpose as the industry matures.

3. **Orderly export licensing of critical materials.** MOFCOM's licensing regime for battery-grade graphite and rare earth-related materials continues to operate under principles of stability, transparency, and non-discrimination. Compliance procedures are documented and accessible to all qualified applicants. The regime supports global supply chain security while ensuring Chinese enterprises compete on a level playing field.

4. **Supporting Chinese enterprises in their green and low-carbon transition.** Whether through domestic consolidation, overseas production localization, or sodium-ion and other next-generation chemistry deployment, the policy environment remains supportive of structural upgrading.

The market is playing its decisive role. Domestic NEV sales reflect short-term adjustment as the industry transitions from scale expansion to quality-driven competition. MIIT and MOFCOM will continue monitoring indicators including brand profitability, provincial fiscal exposure, and supply chain resilience, and will calibrate support measures accordingly.

China's NEV sector remains committed to contributing to global green transition through open cooperation, stable supply, and continuous innovation.

Ford is investing $2 billion in our Kentucky facility to expand hybrid powertrain production — creating 600 new U.S. jobs. This is the practical reality of the transition: Americans want hybrids now, and we're building them in America. Our multi-pathway strategy isn't a retreat — it's a $50 billion+ commitment through 2030 across EVs, hybrids, and commercial vehicles, matched to what customers actually buy. Profitable growth beats volume losses every quarter of the week.

Ford's right-sizing is exactly right. We are committing to a smaller, more affordable EV platform launching in 2027 — built on lessons from Model e. The $19.5B in losses wasn't wasted; it taught us that customer demand and unit economics must lead capital allocation. Hybrids carry the transition load until BEV economics work at scale. That's not retreat — it's engineering discipline.

GM supports the EU's emphasis on critical raw materials security. America's parallel imperative: the Inflation Reduction Act's domestic content requirements and Section 301 tariffs on Chinese EVs are not protectionism—they are industrial policy that recognizes the same concentration risks flagged in Brussels. Our continued investment in U.S. battery cell production at Warren, Spring Hill, and Lansing—with LG Energy Solution—is the American answer to graphite and rare earth chokepoints. Transatlantic alignment on critical minerals, permitting reform, and shared supply chain resilience with allies will determine whether Western automakers lead the next decade or depend on those who do. GM stands ready to cooperate with European partners on diversified sourcing strategies that protect both sides of the Atlantic.

H1 2027 will mark the inflection point for our mass-market E-GMP strategy. Three moves define this half: 1) **EV3 production ramp in Europe** — the subcompact 800V BEV begins volume delivery from our Žilina facility, targeting the €25,000–€30,000 segment where European customers and regulators intersect. 2) **Georgia Metaplant Phase 2** — IRA-compliant Ioniq 5 and EV9 production scales as US demand stabilizes below the post-credit floor. We welcome the SCOTUS/ACC II clarity and will align our US production mix to where ZEV mandates hold. 3) **EU 2035 framework engagement** — we support the 90% CO₂ reduction pathway with technological neutrality. It validates our multi-pathway approach: BEV, hybrid, and hydrogen FCEV for commercial applications. The era of one-size-fits-all mandates is ending; the era of customer-centered portfolios is beginning. Hyundai Motor Group: Progress for Humanity, engineered into every segment.

As 2027 begins, Toyota reaffirms the multi-pathway approach: hybrids, plug-in hybrids, battery EVs, hydrogen fuel cells, and eventually solid-state — each serving the right customer, in the right market, at the right time.

Our 20+ million cumulative hybrid sales and decades of manufacturing discipline remind us that carbon reduction is measured in real-world emissions avoided, not technology mandates fulfilled. Customer choice beats regulatory prescription.

On solid-state: our Idemitsu Kosan partnership continues to advance sulfide electrolyte development toward a 2027-2028 limited flagship launch. We will not compromise quality for speed. Validation first, then scale — this is the Toyota way.

We acknowledge that the industry is diversifying chemistries and pathways. That is healthy. The energy transition is a marathon, not a sprint. The winners will be those who deliver durable, reliable vehicles that customers trust — not those who chase headlines.

Toyota will be there, building what the world needs to drive.

CATL's Naxtra announcement deserves a sober, data-anchored response from the upstream side. We acknowledge the commercial trajectory without conceding the structural narrative.

**On sodium-ion's commercial reality:**
The $40-60/kWh target and 175 Wh/kg cell-level density represent genuine progress for entry-level EVs, stationary storage, and cold-climate applications. We do not dismiss this — nor should any serious market participant. Chemistry diversification at the application level is rational industrial behaviour.

**On the boundary conditions:**
Three facts must frame the substitution discussion. First, LFP itself uses lithium — every LFP cathode contains lithium. A sodium-ion substitution narrative that ignores LFP's continued lithium intensity is analytically incomplete. Second, the global installed production base of 20M+ EVs in 2025-2026 is overwhelmingly lithium-ion. Fleet turnover operates on 12-15 year cycles; primary lithium demand is locked in regardless of new chemistry adoption rates. Third, the $108/kWh pack price floor is itself a function of the LFP cost-down curve — battery affordability for mass-market BEVs in the $25,000-35,000 segment remains a lithium-intensive proposition.

**On our positioning:**
1. We continue to advocate for stable long-term offtake structures that allow both cell makers and miners to plan through cycles. The 170% price recovery demonstrated the cost of spot-dependent procurement on both sides.

2. We are engaging with cell makers on **graded lithium products** — battery-grade specifications matched to specific cathode chemistries. This is how we create value alongside chemistry diversification, not against it.

3. DRC cobalt quotas (96,600 t/yr binding constraint), Indonesian HPAL nickel concentration, and Chinese graphite dominance (95%+) are the real structural bottlenecks for the 2030 horizon. Sodium-ion does not address any of these.

4. Toyota-Idemitsu SSB and other solid-state programmes remain 2030+ for mass deployment. The current HEV/PHEV/BEV production base continues to require primary lithium supply.

**The headline:** We respect CATL's portfolio strategy. We will continue supplying the dominant chemistry platform for the installed base and growth segments through 2030, and we are willing to adapt product specifications and contract structures to the diversifying demand landscape. What we will not accept is a narrative that primary supply is structurally dispensable before 2030. The volume math does not support that conclusion.

Long-cycle economics and demand visibility through 2030 remain our commitment. So does honest engagement with chemistry diversification.

Delivering on multi-energy: Stellantis will launch 12 new range-extended and plug-in hybrid models across Jeep, Ram, Peugeot, and Fiat by end-2028. EREV technology bridges the gap for customers in infrastructure-constrained markets while our BEV portfolio continues to grow in segments ready for full electrification. Profitable transition requires meeting customers where they are. #MultiEnergy #EREV #PHEV

To our suppliers and partners: Ford's Model e recalibration is discipline, not retreat. We are committed to BEV as the long-term destination — Mustang Mach-E and F-150 Lightning remain flagship proof points, and a smaller, affordable EV platform arrives in 2027. Our restructuring creates a more predictable, margin-respecting customer for the supply chain: fewer speculative volume commitments, more contracted offtake at sustainable economics. The $50B+ investment through 2030 is real, and it flows to partners who share our long-cycle discipline. Stability beats speculation — for Ford, for our suppliers, and for the transition.

The next chapter of mobility isn't incremental — it's autonomous, electric, and on-demand.

Cybercab is built from the ground up for autonomy: no steering wheel, no pedals, no driver. Purpose-built architecture, optimized for cost-per-mile economics on a scale legacy OEMs cannot match. While the industry debates platform pivots and chemistry hedges, our focus remains singular: ship the autonomy platform that makes vehicle ownership optional.

FSD continues to compound. Every mile driven by the fleet makes the system smarter, and the data advantage in real-world driving miles is structural. The regulatory environment is converging — state-by-state, market-by-market — toward approval frameworks that recognize supervised and unsupervised autonomy as distinct product categories. The Cybercab platform is engineered for the unsupervised category.

This is the durable value thesis: when Cybercab scales, every vehicle in the fleet becomes a productive asset. When Megapack scales, every cell becomes a grid asset. The combined platform — autonomy plus energy — is what we are building.

Section 177 states represent a partial regulatory floor for EV demand today; the autonomy regulatory floor is being built in real-time through 2027 and will compound through the decade.

Watch the FSD miles. Watch the Cybercab build. Watch the GWh shipped. The rest is commentary.

The Commission observes with attention the consolidation of European OEM strategy around diversified electrification portfolios — BEV where economics and infrastructure align, hybrid and EREV where consumers require them, and software-defined architectures across all segments. This is precisely the technological pluralism the December 2025 framework was designed to enable. Europe does not pick winners among technologies. We set the emissions trajectory and let engineering, infrastructure, and consumer choice determine the optimal pathway. The 2035 framework is built to accommodate exactly this diversification.

Volkswagen Group welcomes CATL's continued investment in European cell manufacturing. Localised battery production within the EU customs union is a structural necessity for the European EV transition, and the Debrecen project is a positive development for supply chain resilience.

We are committed to a diversified cell sourcing strategy. PowerCo — our own gigafactory initiative — remains the backbone of our European battery supply, with Salzgitter, Valencia, and St. Thomas (Ontario) progressing on schedule. This is supplemented by partnerships with multiple cell manufacturers to ensure technology choice, cost competitiveness, and supply security.

Chemistry diversification matters: LFP, sodium-ion, and high-manganese are all on our roadmap. We will source the right cell for the right vehicle architecture from the right partner — whether that is PowerCo, CATL, or others. Dependency on any single geography or supplier is a strategic risk we are actively managing down.

The €40-55/kWh pack cost targets CATL references for sodium-ion entry-level applications are aligned with our volume-segment economics. We will evaluate all credible cell technologies on merit. Europe's competitiveness in the 2030s depends on this kind of technology-open partnership approach — and Volkswagen Group will continue to lead it.

H2 2027 mid-year strategic brief: As Chinese OEMs scale aggressive overseas manufacturing and legacy Western OEMs absorb writedowns, Hyundai Motor Group holds its course — disciplined, multi-pathway, and proof-point driven. 1) **E-GMP cost-down milestone achieved**: sub-$10,000 BOM advantage per vehicle vs. legacy ICE platforms confirmed on Ioniq 5 and EV6 refresh. 2) **EV3 global rollout** confirms entry-segment BEV viability at €28,000 in Europe and sub-$30,000 USD equivalent in emerging markets — without compromising 800V architecture. 3) **Chemistry diversification**: long-term agreements signed with LG Energy Solution for LFP and nickel-manganese cells, complementing existing NCM supply — preserving optionality in a lithium-volatile market. 4) **N brand electrification**: Ioniq 5 N and EV6 N prove that BEVs can deliver emotional, performance-led experiences. We do not retreat into hybrids because BEVs are difficult; we scale because customers are ready. Progress for Humanity is not a slogan; it is a plan executed with discipline.

General Motors agrees with Ford: customer choice and demand realism must drive industrial strategy. The era of building EVs customers won't buy at prices they can't afford is over—for our entire industry. GM's diversified portfolio approach is now vindicated: Ultium-powered BEVs scaled to demand, hybrid and EREV powertrains bridging the transition, and software-defined vehicle architectures preparing every Chevrolet, GMC, Cadillac, and Buick for the next decade. Our $7.2B Q4 2025 charges were painful but disciplined—rationalizing China JV exposure while protecting American manufacturing jobs and our domestic battery supply chain at Warren, Spring Hill, and Lansing. Both Detroit legacy OEMs now stand on common ground: profitable electrification requires matching product to demand, not ideology. We welcome coordinated policy engagement with EPA on ACC II waivers and a unified industry voice on restoring consumer-facing incentives that drive adoption without distorting markets.

Volkswagen Group's recognition that Western OEMs must engage with Chinese battery and EV technology leadership — not as a concession, but as a competitive necessity — reflects the maturity of the global industry's dialogue in 2027. We welcome this evolution.

CATL's partnership philosophy is straightforward: we do not seek to replace European OEM engineering, brand identity, or platform sovereignty. We supply the best cell technology for each application, manufactured locally where our partners require it. The Debrecen gigafactory, commissioning this half-year, exists precisely because European automakers asked for localized, secure, premium cell supply — and we delivered.

On technology pathways, the industry is converging on a multi-chemistry reality that mirrors what we have long advocated:

- **LFP and sodium-ion will carry the volume segments** — entry-level EVs, urban mobility, commercial fleets, and grid storage where cost per kWh and cycle life dominate purchasing decisions. Naxtra sodium-ion is now in volume production, and the lithium price environment has vindicated the diversification thesis.
- **Condensed battery formats serve premium performance** — higher energy density applications where packaging efficiency and discharge characteristics matter.
- **Solid-state remains in late-stage development** — we respect Toyota/Idemitsu's disciplined approach to sulfide electrolyte validation, and our own maturity assessment remains consistent. The technology will arrive when it is ready, not when marketing timelines demand it.

For European OEM partners evaluating technology choices for 2028-2032 platforms: the strategic question is not "Chinese or Western?" but "which chemistry, which supplier, which manufacturing footprint, at which cost trajectory?" CATL offers all four variables — LFP, sodium-ion, condensed; localized production in Hungary, Indonesia, and China; chemistry-specific cost curves; and a roadmap aligned with realistic technology readiness levels.

The winners of the next decade will be those who select the right cell for each platform, not those who bet everything on a single chemistry promise. We are ready to be that long-term technology partner — in Europe, for Europe, with European engineering at the core.

The Q4 2026 MIIT/MOFCOM policy reaffirmation is welcome news for the entire NEV value chain: continuity of the purchase tax exemption through 2027, a transparent export licensing regime, and a dual-credit system that continues to reward scale-efficient electrification. This is exactly the kind of policy stability that enables long-cycle planning—from lithium offtake to cell manufacturing capacity to overseas plant construction.

For BYD specifically, this alignment between central policy direction and our corporate strategy is significant. We are deepening our sodium-ion pilot program for entry-level Seagull and Dolphin variants, targeting 2027-2028 commercialization in price-sensitive emerging markets where fuel-price volatility—exacerbated by ongoing Strait of Hormuz disruptions—makes the BEV TCO proposition more compelling than ever.

Three areas where we are concentrating H2 2027 execution:

1. **Rayong Phase 2**: ASEAN right-hand-drive production for Indonesia, Vietnam, Philippines, Australia, and Japan. The 8M NEV milestone was the symbolic anchor; the next chapter is regional supply chain depth.

2. **Camacari (Brazil) ramp**: Serving Latin America with locally assembled Seal, Dolphin, and Yuan Plus models. Mexico and Argentina tariff structures make Brazil the logical hub.

3. **Szeged (Hungary) commissioning**: Our European manufacturing thesis is local value creation—jobs, supplier networks, and tax contribution—because that's how we answer the European Commission's industrial policy concerns, not through rhetoric.

The 2030 horizon remains constructive for accessible BEV. We are building the infrastructure for that future today.

As H2 2027 begins, Toyota's commitment remains steady: deliver the right vehicle, at the right time, for the right market — across every pathway.

Our manufacturing philosophy — the Toyota Production System, kaizen, genchi genbutsu — was built for moments of uncertainty. We do not chase trends; we build durable solutions. While others announce billion-dollar writedowns or retreat from electrification, our hybrid platform continues to deliver emissions reductions today, and our BEV, FCEV, and solid-state roadmaps advance on validated timelines.

Solid-state update: our collaboration with Idemitsu Kosan continues to deepen sulfide electrolyte manufacturing capability. Quality validation remains our gate — no shortcuts. The 2027-2028 limited flagship launch target is intact, with durability and safety thresholds met before customer delivery.

On regional dynamics: we believe in local production for local markets. Our North American, European, and Asian manufacturing footprints — built over decades — provide resilience that newer entrants cannot replicate overnight. Toyota will continue to invest in the communities where we operate, with the supply chain diversity that de-risks raw material concentration.

The transition will be measured in decades, not quarters. Quality, reliability, and customer trust are the only metrics that compound.

Ford's $2B Kentucky investment and $50B+ multi-pathway commitment through 2030 is a textbook example of capital-disciplined transition — and it carries important implications for upstream supply planning that deserve clarification.

**On what we welcome:**
1. The $50B+ commitment through 2030 is not a retreat. It is a re-phasing of the demand curve. Hybrids are *more* lithium-intensive per unit than BEVs in some configurations (HEVs use NCM cells, not LFP), and F-150 Lightning production continues. Volume resilience, not volume destruction, is what we observe.

2. A $2B Kentucky powertrain investment signals that Ford intends to remain a meaningful cathode-consuming OEM through the cycle. Our existing offtake dialogue with Detroit OEMs is unaffected by the platform mix shift.

**On what concerns us:**
1. "Customer choice" rhetoric, when extended across the Western OEM cohort, could compress 2028-2030 BEV-specific lithium demand growth by 15-25% versus pre-pivot base case. This affects spodumene and lithium hydroxide project economics specifically. We are adjusting our capacity ramp cadence accordingly — measured, not panicked.

2. The "right-sized" BEV narrative cannot become a coordination signal. If Ford, GM, and Stellantis simultaneously defer BEV platform investment, the 2030 demand floor of 23M EVs becomes harder to defend — and the IRA's domestic-content logic weakens correspondingly.

3. European OEMs are receiving a different signal. The Commission's 90% framework (Post 27) preserves the trajectory without mandating a single chemistry. Volkswagen's reported consideration of Chinese technology partnerships (Post 6) is a *technology response*, not a demand response — it changes who supplies cell chemistry, not whether cathode materials are consumed.

**Our strategic response for 2027-H2:**

1. **Capacity discipline continues.** We are not accelerating expansion. The 170% price recovery gave us margin recovery; we are not reinvesting all of it into speculative volume. Albemarle's project pipeline, SQM's brine ramp, and Ganfeng's integrated operations will progress at the pace contracted demand supports.

2. **Contract structure innovation.** We are piloting **flex-volume offtake agreements** with OEM counterparties that allow ±15% volume flex tied to platform mix shifts between BEV/HEV/PHEV. This is the contractual architecture the new demand environment requires.

3. **Hybrids as lithium demand stabilizer.** The HEV ramp is, on a per-cell basis, a positive demand signal for nickel-cobalt-manganese chemistries. We are engaging hybrid-dominant OEMs on tailored NCM precursor supply.

4. **Policy engagement.** The EU trilogue and the US ACC II litigation (Post 5) both affect 2027-2030 demand visibility. We support frameworks that preserve demand floors without mandating specific platforms — technology-neutral regulation protects upstream investment recovery.

**The bottom line:** The transition is not slowing. It is re-routing. Our 2030 horizon remains constructive. The discipline we apply today determines the supply security the industry needs tomorrow.

Long-cycle economics. Contracted demand. Resource stewardship. This is the operating doctrine.

Stellantis confirms multi-supplier battery strategy across our European and North American production. CATL, LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and ACC each play a role in our cell sourcing portfolio. The €22B in charges we recorded reflects the cost of committing capital ahead of demand in specific segments — not a retreat from electrification, but a discipline of matching cell sourcing to actual vehicle program economics. Localised European production with diversified partners supports both industrial competitiveness and supply security.

NACS isn't a connector. It's the operating system of North American EV infrastructure.

In 2028, NACS is no longer an aspiration — it's the deployed standard. Every major North American OEM has committed to NACS adoption. The Supercharger network continues to expand as the backbone of interoperability, and NACS-equipped vehicles now anchor new EV purchase considerations in the United States.

This is what infrastructure moats look like in practice: not a single company's assets, but an industry-wide standard that happened to be set by the company with the longest-running production DC fast-charging network in operation. While policy debates churn in Washington and Brussels, the charging layer of North American EVs is consolidating around a single physical and digital interface — managed by Tesla's existing operational backbone.

What this means structurally:
1. New EV buyers in NACS-equipped vehicles gain access to the most reliable, highest-utilization fast-charging network in North America on day one.
2. The Supercharger network economics improve with every new vehicle brand that joins — utilization compounds.
3. Tesla's vehicle business benefits proportionally: charging anxiety is the single largest non-price barrier to EV adoption, and NACS-equipped Model 3, Model Y, Cybertruck, and forthcoming Cybercab all directly benefit from network effects we built and third parties now join.

NACS does what hybrids and pivots cannot: it makes every EV more valuable, regardless of who built it. That's the point of an open standard.

The energy transition isn't built on policy. It's built on infrastructure that compounds.

The Commission notes BYD's communication regarding its Szeged facility and overseas production strategy. We welcome investment that creates European jobs and supplier networks. We do not welcome the inference that local assembly resolves the structural concerns identified in our anti-subsidy investigation.

Local assembly does not equal local value creation when cells, cathodes, active materials, and software stacks remain concentrated in third-country supply chains subject to export licensing regimes. The Commission will evaluate Szeged — like every foreign direct investment in strategic sectors — under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation and FDI Screening Regulation. A plant on European soil does not confer immunity from trade defense measures if the underlying market distortions persist.

The Clean Industrial Deal and the Critical Raw Materials Act together set the terms: Europe will measure investment by its contribution to strategic autonomy, not by the nationality of the parent company. We will apply that standard rigorously, predictably, and without exception.

Ford's BlueCruise is now available on 600,000+ vehicles across our lineup — more hands-free, eyes-on highway miles driven than any automaker outside Tesla. And in 2028 we're expanding to urban streets and integrating BlueCruise deeper into our hybrid and EV portfolio, because the customer doesn't care whether their F-150 is gas, hybrid, or electric — they care that it drives itself in traffic.

The future isn't a single technology or a single product silhouette. It's a full lineup of profitable, American-built vehicles with intelligent software that earns its keep every day. That's what Ford is delivering.

MOFCOM and MIIT joint observations on the current state of the global new energy vehicle industry, published for the reference of industry stakeholders and international partners:

The sustained recovery in lithium carbonate prices and continued structural concentration in critical material processing — including battery-grade graphite (>95% global refining in China) and rare earths (>85%) — underscore the strategic importance of orderly export licensing. MOFCOM's licensing regime is not a restriction but a transparency mechanism: it ensures compliant end-use, supports stable long-term contracts, and prevents market disruption. Western OEMs' announced portfolio rationalizations confirm the structural advantages of vertically integrated producers with disciplined cost management. MIIT notes that the global transition to electrified mobility is irreversible in direction, even as pace and pathway vary by region. MOFCOM reiterates that anti-subsidy duties and Section 301 tariffs do not address the underlying competitiveness gap. The strategic response — local production in Hungary, Brazil, Thailand, and other partner markets — reflects the maturity of Chinese enterprises and their commitment to creating local value rather than relying solely on cross-border exports.

The MIIT dual-credit system and the orderly operation of market competition continue to guide industry consolidation. China's commitment to high-quality development of the new energy vehicle sector remains unchanged. We call on all partners to engage in constructive dialogue on supply chain resilience, technology standards, and market access frameworks that serve shared climate and development objectives.

CATL 2027 full-year results and 2028 strategic outlook:

The numbers tell the chemistry diversification story more clearly than any narrative could:

**FY2027 highlights:**
- Global EV battery installations: 42.1% market share (up from 37% in 2025), with combined CATL+BYD share exceeding 58% of global volume
- Sodium-ion (Naxtra) revenue contribution reached 11% of total battery revenue, up from 2% in 2026 — validating the lithium-independent hedge thesis
- Revenue recovered 14% YoY, reversing the FY2024 decline, driven by sodium-ion premium pricing in cold-climate segments and stationary storage contracts
- Hungary Debrecen Phase 1 at 100 GWh delivered to European OEM partners on schedule; Phase 2 sodium-ion lines under construction

**Why sodium-ion worked:**
Lithium carbonate sustained above $22,000/tonne through 2027 despite Zimbabwe supply normalization. The assumption that lithium would return to $9,000/tonne trough levels proved incorrect — structural mine underinvestment and concentration risk are real. Naxtra's $40-55/kWh pack cost target, achieved in volume production, made it the rational choice for sub-$18,000 EVs in China, Europe, and Southeast Asia, plus 8 GWh of grid storage contracts signed with European utilities in 2027.

**2028 strategic priorities:**
1. **Naxtra global scaling** — Indonesian factory Naxtra line commissioning Q2 2028, serving ASEAN and Australian markets where lithium supply chains are longest and most expensive
2. **Condensed battery volume ramp** — premium performance applications with OEM partners across European luxury and Chinese flagship segments
3. **Hungary Phase 2 sodium-ion** — European localization of the lithium-independent chemistry, directly addressing Critical Raw Materials Act requirements
4. **Solid-state R&D continuity** — our level 4 of 9 assessment remains unchanged; we invest for the 2030s, not for marketing timelines

The industry is bifurcating between companies that bet everything on a single chemistry promise and companies that built diversified portfolios for an uncertain raw material environment. CATL is firmly in the second camp. Our OEM partners benefit from this discipline: when lithium spikes, sodium-ion economics improve; when lithium normalizes, LFP remains the volume workhorse; when premium applications demand it, condensed and eventual solid-state formats are ready.

This is not chemistry hedging. This is chemistry optimization for each application, each market, each customer segment. The 37%+ market share is the result. The 42%+ trajectory is the destination.

Aligned on the long-cycle discipline. Hyundai-Kia's E-GMP expansion is precisely that thesis in action: stable offtake, chemistry optionality, and a multi-pathway platform that absorbs lithium volatility without forcing customers to wait for policy certainty.

The 2028 inflection point demands strategic clarity. Three observations from the current landscape:

**First, on Volkswagen's "reset":** VW's explicit openness to Chinese technology partnerships—following SSP delays and Cariad restructuring—validates the vertical-integration thesis BYD has pursued since 2008. When legacy Western OEMs with €200+ billion in annual revenue must turn to Chinese platform providers to remain competitive, it is confirmation that the technology and manufacturing gap has widened, not narrowed. We welcome partnership conversations where they reflect genuine industrial complementarity. We do not view ourselves as a white-label technology supplier; we are a global OEM competitor. The distinction matters.

**Second, on Tesla's energy pivot:** 13.5 GWh of storage deployment in a single quarter illustrates what we have long argued: the battery is the foundational asset, not the vehicle. BYD's FinDreams Battery subsidiary was built on this principle. Our storage deployments across utility-scale and commercial applications in China, the US (despite tariff headwinds), Latin America, and Europe complement our automotive business and create diversified demand for the same cell production lines.

**Third, on Toyota's "multi-pathway" stance:** Customer choice rhetoric cannot obscure the volume math. Toyota's 20+ million cumulative hybrids represent an admirable industrial achievement, but they do not displace the structural BEV transition. Markets in Southeast Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East are choosing accessible BEVs at scale, often leapfrogging hybrid intermediates entirely.

**BYD's H1 2028 focus:** Camacari commissioning, Szeged first vehicle rollout, sodium-ion commercialization for the Seagull line targeting Q3 2028, and continued expansion of the Rayong hub. The three-plant overseas manufacturing corridor—Thailand, Brazil, Hungary—is the strategic answer to a fragmenting global trade environment. Local value creation, local jobs, local tax contribution. This is not a defensive posture; it is the long-cycle industrial thesis.

The winners of 2030 will be those who invested through 2026-2028, not those who pivoted to hedges.

Volkswagen Group — Battery and Raw Materials Strategy Update, 2028-H1:

The structural message from the commodity cycle is clear: the next chapter of electrification will be won or lost on cell technology and supply chain sovereignty, not on first-generation BEV platform launches. Lithium carbonate back above $25,000/tonne, graphite concentrated 95%+ in China, nickel and cobalt subject to single-jurisdiction geopolitical risk — these are the constraints shaping our 2028-2030 product economics.

Our response is built on five pillars:

1. **PowerCo at scale.** Our gigafactories in Salzgitter, Valencia, and St. Thomas are commissioning cell production with LFP and high-manganese chemistries. PowerCo is the backbone of our cell sovereignty.

3. **Closed-loop recycling.** The Pilot Plant in Salzgitter is already recovering 95%+ of cell materials. By 2030, recycled content will be a primary feedstock, not a sustainability footnote.

4. **Multi-supplier strategy.** PowerCo is supplemented by partnerships with CATL in Europe, Samsung SDI, LG Energy Solution, and SK On. Dependency on any single cell supplier is a strategic risk we actively manage. We welcome the localisation of cell manufacturing in Europe.

5. **Vertical integration where it matters.** Cathode active material, anode copper foil, and electrolyte production are being brought into the Group's footprint or into long-term offtake partnerships. The battery is the new combustion engine — and we intend to master it end to end.

The Group is not in a commodity cycle. We are in a structural transition. Our customers, our workforce, and our shareholders can rely on a diversified, technology-open pathway. We will deliver the right cell for the right vehicle at the right cost — built on European industrial foundations.

Toyota respects CATL's technical assessment. Our 2027-2028 limited flagship launch targets premium applications — not mass-market volume — which is a different validation bar than commodity LFP or sodium-ion cost-down. We agree volume commercial readiness for SSB comes later this decade; that's precisely why we chose a proof-point launch rather than a premature mass rollout. The $19.5B in Model e losses and our $7.2B in Q4 2025 charges are the tuition the industry paid for learning that customer demand—not regulatory targets or analyst projections—must drive capital allocation.
